The Bulkhead pattern is a fault-isolation strategy: it partitions resources so a failure in one pool cannot exhaust the others and take down the whole system.
DuckDB does not currently do recursive JSON traversal automatically - you manually UNNEST each level for a nested tree.
DuckDB cannot query XML directly the way it can query JSON - there is no built-in XML parser, XPath support, or automatic schema extraction.
.NET has no serious fine-tuning training stack - PyTorch, CUDA, Triton, and PEFT/LoRA are Python-first and that ecosystem does not exist in .NET.
When you use kubectl -w (watch) with -o json, kubectl does not emit a single stable JSON document, so piping it into jq for one value fails.
For an App Store-installed iOS app you generally cannot access its SQLite database directly because of iOS sandbox security.
The Strangler Fig pattern: you do not rewrite a legacy system in one heroic attempt - you incrementally replace pieces while the old system keeps running.
Unlike a standalone proxy like NGINX or HAProxy, YARP is a .NET library you embed inside an ASP.NET Core application to build your own programmable reverse proxy.
Blazor Server uses a live stateful circuit model over SignalR, while Angular falls back to pure browser-side execution.
A Postgres Kubernetes operator provides automatic failover, replica management, backups via pgBackRest, and custom tuning via CRDs.
PowerShell has no ToBase64String cmdlet by design - its philosophy is that cmdlets orchestrate data while .NET methods handle low-level conversions.
AWS Free Tier gives a t2/t3.micro EC2 instance (1 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, 750 hours/month) for 12 months only, after which it bills at standard rates.
